listening.passage:
Teacher: How does your class use new media for school projects?
Maha: We use a class platform to share ideas and documents. We also use video calls when a group member is absent.
Teacher: How do you decide whether online information is reliable?
Maha: First, I check the source. I look for the author and the date, and I compare important information with another reliable website.
Teacher: What about screen time?
Maha: I try not to use my phone late at night because it can affect my sleep. During study time, I turn off unnecessary notifications.
Teacher: Do you think social media is useful?
Maha: Yes, if we use it responsibly. It helps us communicate quickly, but we should protect our privacy and think before posting.
Teacher: What is your most important rule?
Maha: I never share private information or a photograph of someone without permission.

Presenter: Welcome to Voices at School. Today we are talking to Maha about Spotlight, a film project exploring what fame means to teenagers. Why did your group start it?

Presenter: Who did you interview first?
Maha: A young musician called Sami. He enjoys performing, but he explained that constant messages from strangers sometimes made him uncomfortable. He never shares his home address online.
Presenter: When did you begin planning?
Maha: We started in September. First we asked students to suggest questions, then our teacher helped us choose the most respectful ones.
Presenter: What went wrong on the day of filming?
Maha: A power cut interrupted the recording. Instead of cancelling, we moved to a bright room near the courtyard and used a battery-powered recorder.
Presenter: How long was the finished documentary?
Maha: Just three minutes. We cut repeated details because we wanted the message to be clear. Editing took longer than filming.
Presenter: Did you post the interviews immediately?
Maha: No. Everyone watched their clip first and gave permission before we shared anything. Two people asked us to remove personal information, and we respected their wishes.

My name is Salma, and I want to describe an experience connected with coastal research. It started in October when the school environment club agreed to organise an activity at a marine research station near Sur.

Our original plan was a large outdoor survey. We thought it would be simple because several volunteers were enthusiastic, but we soon realised that careful organisation would matter more than confidence alone.

We arranged the main session for Tuesday at nine in the morning. Before anyone arrived, Dr Huda checked our timetable and explained why every participant needed to know who was responsible for each task.

I was responsible for bringing a portable water-testing kit. Other students prepared instructions, checked the equipment and contacted local fishermen to ask what they needed most from the project.

The first difficulty was unexpected: high waves prevented the boat trip. We considered cancelling, but that would have meant losing all the planning and missing a chance to learn from the experience.

Instead, the researchers moved the activity to a sheltered harbour. Our revised plan was a smaller supervised investigation. It was less dramatic than the first idea, but it was safer and easier for everyone to understand.

At the end of the session, the team measured water quality and submitted a report. We recorded both positive comments and criticism, because an honest report should describe limitations as well as achievements.

For me, the main lesson was that reliable evidence matters more than a quick guess. We have already discussed a public exhibition at the school library as a possible follow-up, but we will not announce a date until the planning is finished.

Before the activity began, the organisers asked local fishermen what they would find useful. Their suggestions changed the timetable and helped the group focus on practical details instead of making assumptions.

The team also discussed safety, cost and accessibility with Dr Huda. Although the first proposal seemed attractive, they recognised that a successful project needed reliable information and careful supervision.

During the project, Salma kept a record of dates, decisions and questions. This made it easier to explain the results to visitors who had not been present at the earlier meetings.

Some volunteers disagreed about how much time should be spent on preparation. After a respectful discussion, they agreed to divide the tasks into smaller stages and review their progress at the end of each week.
